name: Planet Organic (Westbourne Grove)
who: Organic supermarket chain founded 1995, now around ten London stores under founder ownership.
why: Pioneered UK organic-supermarket retail; survived a 2023 insolvency and relaunched smaller under its original founders.
warning: Entered administration in May 2023; sold to a company backed by its founders, with four of fourteen stores closed in the process.
takeaway: Go for the pioneer of UK organic-supermarket retail, now smaller and founder-run again after its 2023 near-collapse.

name: Whole Foods Market Kensington
who: The UK's largest Whole Foods Market, occupying the former Barkers department store on Kensington High Street.
why: The chain's most architecturally significant UK site; the grand food-hall building pulls in visitors beyond weekly shoppers.
takeaway: Go for the grand former Barkers department-store building — the UK's biggest, most architecturally striking Whole Foods.

name: As Nature Intended
who: Independent London health-food retailer running six shops (Chiswick, Ealing, Balham, Spitalfields, Stratford, Marble Arch) plus a web shop.
why: A rare independent multi-site health-food group that has kept expanding across London while bigger names struggled.
takeaway: Go for a rare independent that kept expanding to six London shops while bigger health-food names struggled.

name: Infinity Foods
who: Workers' co-operative wholefood shop and bakery trading since 1971, one of Britain's oldest surviving co-ops.
why: Founding-era co-op culture, still worker-owned and run on collective decision-making more than five decades on.
takeaway: One of Britain's oldest surviving co-ops — go for the bakery and the collective decision-making, unchanged since 1971.

name: Unicorn Grocery
who: Worker-owned wholefood co-op in Chorlton, trading since 1996, known for bulk organic produce and affordable pricing.
why: A model of co-operative retail with a genuinely loyal local membership and strict ethical-sourcing standards.
takeaway: Go for bulk organic produce at genuinely affordable prices, run on strict ethical-sourcing standards since 1996.

name: Real Foods
who: Scotland's longest-running organic and special-diet retailer, with two shops on Broughton Street and Brougham Street.
why: A pioneer of natural and special-diet retail in Scotland that has stayed independently run since the 1970s.
takeaway: Go for Scotland's longest-running special-diet retailer, independently run since the 1970s across two Edinburgh shops.

name: Daylesford Organic (Kingham farm shop)
who: Organic farm shop built around Carole Bamford's Cotswolds farm, with an on-site creamery, café and cookery school.
why: Britain's best-known organic farm-shop destination; set the template for farm-to-table retail as a day out.
takeaway: Britain's benchmark organic farm shop — go for the creamery, café and cookery school as a full day out.

name: Naturalia (Boulevard Magenta)
who: France's pioneering organic supermarket chain, opened on Boulevard Magenta in 1973 and now over 250 stores nationwide.
why: One of Europe's first organic-supermarket concepts; helped move organic food from niche shop to mainstream aisle.
takeaway: Go for the store that helped move organic food from niche shop to mainstream French supermarket aisle.

name: La Vie Claire (original Paris shop)
who: France's first organic and health-food store network, founded in 1948, now a nationwide franchise of small shops.
why: Legacy claim to being Europe's original modern health-food retailer, decades ahead of the organic-supermarket boom.
takeaway: Go to see the shop with a claim to being Europe's original modern health-food retailer, since 1948.

name: Alnatura Super Natur Markt (Darmstadt)
who: Flagship 'Super Natur Markt' of Germany's biggest organic brand, sited on Alnatura's landmark clay-and-timber headquarters campus.
why: Showcase store for Alnatura's sustainable-building philosophy; the campus itself is a minor architectural destination.
takeaway: Go for the building as much as the groceries — a showcase of Alnatura's clay-and-timber sustainable architecture.

name: LPG BioMarkt (Prenzlauer Berg)
who: Berlin's oldest organic supermarket chain, trading since 1994, with ten stores and its own organic Ufa bakery.
why: An early mover in German organic retail; its strict regional (200km) sourcing radius sets it apart from national chains.
takeaway: Go for the own bakery and a strict 200km sourcing radius — Berlin's oldest organic supermarket chain.

name: Ekoplaza (plastic-free aisle store)
who: Dutch organic supermarket chain that opened the world's first plastic-free grocery aisle in 2018.
why: Set a global retail precedent for packaging-free organic shopping that other chains have since copied.
takeaway: Go for the world's first plastic-free grocery aisle, the precedent every packaging-free chain since has copied.

name: NaturaSì (Verona)
who: Italy's largest organic supermarket chain, part of the EcorNaturaSì group and rooted in Verona with 300-plus stores.
why: Anchors Italy's organic retail market with strict own-label sourcing standards across a national store network.
takeaway: Go for the own-label sourcing standards anchoring Italy's biggest organic supermarket network, 300-plus stores strong.

name: Negozio Leggero (Turin founding store)
who: The world's first zero-waste, refill-by-weight grocery network, founded in Turin in 2009.
why: Originated the loose-goods refill retail model that zero-waste stores worldwide have since copied.
takeaway: Go to see the founding store of the refill-by-weight model that zero-waste grocers worldwide have since copied.

name: Bio Company
who: Berlin-founded organic supermarket chain (est. 2003), now around sixty stores across northeastern Germany.
why: Scaled Berlin's organic-retail boom into a regional chain while staying independent of the big German grocers.
takeaway: Go for a Berlin-born organic chain that scaled to sixty stores while staying independent of the big grocers.

name: Alara Wholefoods
who: Independent wholefood shop and mill in King's Cross, trading since 1974, known for its own-milled organic flours and refill counters.
why: One of London's longest-running independent health-food shops, having outlasted the wholesale redevelopment of King's Cross around it.
takeaway: Go for own-milled organic flours and refill counters at a shop that outlasted King's Cross redevelopment around it.
